item.title: Month-end FX rebalancing signals favour the dollar - Credit Agricole
item.description:
As if the dollar needed another excuse to stay bid this month. As November trading draws toward a close, we're getting to that time of the month when portfolio rebalancing flows can throw a little spanner in the works for FX traders.

This time around, Credit Agricole's month-end fixing model is pointing to moderate dollar buying across the board, with the strongest buy signal coming against the Swedish krona. The firm notes that:

"Global equity markets were lower across the board in November. In FX, the USD has outperformed across the board on the month. Overall, the moves in equity markets, when adjusted for market capitalisation and FX performance this month, suggest month-end portfolio-rebalancing flows are likely to be moderate USD buying across the board with the strongest buy signal in the case of the USD vs SEK."

For the uninitiated, think of these flows as a bit of housekeeping being done by large fund managers. As the value of their investments changes throughout the month, they may need to buy or sell currencies to bring their portfolio allocations and currency hedges back in line by the end of it.

As such, these flows aren't necessarily a reflection of what the general market backdrop or conviction is playing out to be.

The added complication for November though is that there is also the Thanksgiving holiday thinning out liquidity today and tomorrow. While the month-end fixing on Monday next week will be one to watch, any sizeable orders coming through before then could also have an outsized impact if liquidity conditions remain subdued as that could lead to exacerbated price movements. So, just be wary of that as well over the next two days.

As a reminder, do remember that these flows should not be treated as a hard directional call. They are notoriously difficult to pin down and tend to take on more importance as we get closer to the fix itself. If anything else, think of them as another piece of the puzzle rather than the main driver of price action.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin consolidates at yearly lows as traders await fresh catalyst amid negative backdrop
item.description:
Bitcoin is now consolidating near the yearly lows as traders await new catalysts to pick a direction. The crypto market has been driven mainly by tightening financial conditions and risk-off flows amid intensifying growth concerns.

Keep in mind that higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions are a headwind for risk assets, especially cryptocurrencies, which are sensitive to changes in liquidity and risk appetite.

In terms of fundamentals, nothing has changed. The Fed is still going to raise rates and how much will depend on the economic data and the stock market conditions.

The US-Iran stalemate continues to drag on, and the situation doesn’t look like it’s going to improve anytime soon. Therefore, the macro backdrop remains negative for Bitcoin and the crypto market in general.

Looking ahead, Bitcoin will likely remain skewed to the downside as long as the macro conditions remain unfavourable. For a reversal in the trend, we will likely need a more dovish Fed or an end to the Iran war.

Looking ahead, gold will likely need support from a dovish repricing in interest rate expectations either from weaker data, dovish Fed commentary or an end to the Iran war. But buyers will also need to be aware that a dovish repricing from renewed stock market selloff could lead to more liquidations.

All that being said though, do be reminded that there is a bit of an awkward pause to the dip buying momentum as a whole. The Thanksgiving holiday is upon us and US stock markets are closed today with only an abbreviated session set for tomorrow. In other words, European stocks will be left to fend for themselves over the next two days without much direction from Wall Street.

As such, I would be careful about reading too much into the gains today - especially with thinner liquidity conditions potentially exaggerating market moves in either direction. The rebound yesterday was encouraging and optimistic, but it doesn't undo weeks of technical damage yet.

The bigger test will only come next week when US investors return and we get a better sense of whether there is any conviction behind the latest rebound. In essence, dip buyers have bought themselves some breathing room. Now, can they make it count?

item.title: China hits back at Trump’s latest tariff threat as trade war tensions resurface
item.description:
It looks like a trade war is back on the menu again. Just when markets thought they could afford to spend a little less time worrying about US-China tensions, we're back to the familiar exchange of threats between Washington and Beijing this week.

China's commerce ministry is hitting back at the latest US tariff proposals today, expressing firm opposition to Washington's Section 301 investigation into structural overcapacity.

"China urges the US to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation. China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests."

As a reminder, the US is proposing additional tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners and that includes a 20% tariff on Chinese goods. In doing so, the latest proposal would bring the average effective tariff rate on Chinese goods back up to roughly 31%.

In essence, US president Trump is looking to rebuild his tariffs wall after the Supreme Court struck down earlier levies.

Now, the language from Beijing is a familiar one and something that we have seen a lot of in the past. At the end of the day, there is a difference between threatening retaliation and actually delivering it. On the latter, I'd actually pay more attention on how Beijing might look to hit back through other avenues. To put it more simply, I'm more interested as to when they will start to bring rare earth export restrictions back into the conversation.

As for markets, the timing of all this is hardly ideal. Investors are already wrestling with a rather painful tech selloff and renewed concerns about economic growth. So when you throw in another round of tariffs uncertainty into the mix, it definitely complicates the recovery effort.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: Swiss franc emerges as a quiet winner in the market turmoil
item.description:
Amid all the selling in equities this week, the Swiss franc is quietly emerging as one of the more notable winners in the major currencies space. And considering how other traditional safe havens have been behaving lately, it's not all too surprising to see the appeal of the franc.

Gold is struggling to keep its head above water, while the Japanese yen remains weighed down by fiscal worries and uncertainty surrounding the BOJ policy outlook. So if you're a trader looking to put your money somewhere safe without necessarily piling into the dollar, the franc makes for a rather compelling alternative.

In that regard, EUR/CHF is arguably one of the more interesting charts to watch among major currencies this week. The pair briefly breached below the 0.9100 mark yesterday, taking it to its lowest levels since March. All that before finding some respite from the late turnaround in Wall Street and then keeping steadier today just above the figure level.

That being said, the technical picture isn't exactly encouraging for buyers at the moment. The November recovery stalled around 0.9255-75, with sellers subsequently taking out both the 0.9200 level and the previous swing region around 0.9175.

Right now, it's all on a test of the May lows near the 0.9100 level. A sustained break below that could open the door for a revisit of the March lows near 0.9000.

As for buyers, there is work to do in first needing to get back above the early November lows around 0.9130-35 to start. After which, a push back above 0.9200 would be needed to regain more conviction in search of a stronger rebound.

Putting the technicals aside for a bit, let's not forget about the fact that the SNB won't necessarily be thrilled about a stronger franc. That is especially the case given Switzerland's inflation backdrop, or should I say lack thereof. So, that's a policy risk worth keeping in the back of one's mind.

But for now, I would argue that EUR/CHF is acting as a useful barometer of broader market anxiety. If traders continue to run for cover and gold and the yen aren't offering much shelter, then the franc could find itself with plenty more admirers in the near-term.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: German consumer confidence remains in the doldrums heading into December
item.description:
• Germany December GfK consumer confidence -30.2 vs -29.9 expected
  • Prior -30.8; revised to -30.9

German consumer sentiment edged up heading into December but continues to remain subdued as a whole, according to the latest GfK/NIM survey.

The breakdown shows that economic expectations falling to -1.6 from 2.1 while price expectations also nudged up a little to 2.8 from 1.0 previously. THe only real bright spot is that income expectations improved a little to -13.9 from -15.7 before this. But at the balance, the report is still suggesting that consumer confidence remains in the dumps.

GfK/NIM even noted that the index was "more or less stagnating at a low level" and that doesn't bode well ahead of the Christmas shopping season.

If anything else, this does provide some suggestion to the ECB that the euro area's largest economy is still not exactly recovering all too well despite the more resilient showing in the first half of the year. The second half of the year looks to be one of consolidating and stagnating momentum, which isn't the most ideal situation as inflation pressures remain strong.

For now, policymakers may still get away with another rate hike, or perhaps even two, but the challenge will grow to be greater next year amid higher stagflationary risks potentially.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ policymaker Tamura hints at faster rate hikes, keeps December in focus
item.description:
A 50 bps rate hike by the BOJ? Now, wouldn't that be something?

We're hearing more comments from BOJ policymaker Tamura today and he is not shying away about talking up the prospect of more aggressive rate hikes by the central bank. His latest remarks:

  • I do have an image in mind of raising interest rates once every few months
  • If inflation risks materialise, BOJ may need to speed up pace of rate hikes or even deliver a 50 bps rate hike
  • Stock, asset price moves are among factors we will look at in measuring financial conditions
  • Would look to decide policy by looking at the data, as well as economic, financial developments leading up to December meeting

Before we get too carried away by the headlines though, let's remember who we're dealing with here. Tamura has been one of the leading hawks at the BOJ since joining the central bank in July 2022. So, none of this is particularly out of character.

As such, the more interesting question is whether how other policymakers are feeling and if they are viewing things the same way as Tamura is. For now, there's no real suggestion of any overly hawkish leanings along the same lines at least.

For the most part, the BOJ has already acknowledged that underlying inflation has broadly reached its 2% target. However, they're not explicitly taking any steps or setting out a position to pre-commit to a rate hike for December and also for next year.

As things stand, traders are pricing in roughly 70% odds of a 25 bps rate hike in December. While the odds are solid, they're not exactly screaming conviction just yet. And I doubt Tamura's remarks alone will do much to move the needle on that front.

What would carry more weight is if we start hearing a similar sense of urgency from some of the less hawkish members of the BOJ. That's where I'd be looking for clues in the run-up to the December meeting.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

  • Stocks: the Nikkei rose about 1.6%, the Kospi about 1.5% and the Hang Seng about 1.9%, led by chipmakers, while Shanghai was flat

  • Nvidia ratings: S&P put Nvidia's AA rating on CreditWatch negative, while Moody's held at Aa1
  • Gold: it steadied near $3,590 and Brent traded near $91 after a tanker incident off Dubai

Asian stocks extended their recovery on Thursday, led by chipmakers, as two of the region's central banks struck hawkish tones and US stock futures rose in thin trade with Wall Street closed for Thanksgiving.

Equities: chips lead a second day of gains

Japan's Nikkei 225 rose about 1.6% to around 57,900, adding to its early gains, while the broader Topix rose about 0.5%. South Korea's Kospi climbed about 1.5% and the tech-heavy Kosdaq more than 2%, as SK Hynix gained about 3.5% and Samsung Electronics about 1.7%. The moves recovered part of Wednesday's heavy losses, when the Kospi fell more than 6%.

In China, Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose about 1.9%, while the Shanghai Composite was little changed. US stock index futures built on Wall Street's late rebound on Wednesday, with S&P 500 futures up about 0.7% and Nasdaq 100 futures about 1.1% higher.

Central banks: Seoul hikes, Tokyo hawk pushes

The Bank of Korea raised its base rate by a quarter point to 3.25%, its third hike since July, as expected. The decision drew two dissents, from board members Lee Soo-hyung and Hwang Kun-il, but the board's projections leaned hawkish: 15 of 21 put the rate above 3.25% in six months, including seven at 3.75%. The bank said inflation will stay above target for a prolonged period and that the timing of further hikes will depend on inflation, growth and financial stability. It forecast growth of 3.9% this year and 4.1% in 2027, driven by semiconductor exports.

In Japan, Bank of Japan board member Naoki Tamura said the policy rate should be brought to neutral "soon", repeating his view that neutral is around 2%, well above the current 1.25%. He said the BoJ should "make haste slowly" but be ready to speed up hikes if inflation overshoots. Japanese two-year government bond yields rose about 4 basis points to around 1.76%, while the 10-year yield edged up to around 2.66%. The yen barely moved, with USD/JPY holding near 159.10.

Australia: capex surges

Australian private capital spending jumped 12.2% in the third quarter, almost three times the 4.4% forecast, as equipment investment surged 23.1% to a record, led by the industry that includes data centres. Firms also lifted their spending plans for 2026-27 by 11.8% to about A$224 billion. The Australian dollar rose about 0.3% to around 0.6646.

AI and credit: the stress shifts to governance and funding

S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's AA rating on CreditWatch negative, warning of a possible one-notch downgrade within 90 days over concerns about board independence, key-person risk and export-control questions. Moody's, by contrast, kept its Aa1 rating and stable outlook. Elsewhere, CoreWeave's banks are preparing a $4.5 billion loan backed by a Meta contract, even as the cost of insuring CoreWeave's own debt hit a record. South Africa's central bank warned that AI firms now compete with governments for long-term funding. Resistance to data centre projects is spreading too, from Tokyo's suburbs to Australia's Northern Territory and across the United States.

Sentiment calls were mixed. Citi Wealth said extreme investor fear offers a buying opportunity, Bank of America set a cautious S&P 500 target of 7,800 for the end of 2027, and Goldman Sachs said hedge funds have been adding short positions. Michael Burry closed his remaining bearish bets on the Nasdaq-100 but said he still plans to short Nvidia nearer $200.

Commodities: gold steadies, oil holds gains

Gold held near $3,590 an ounce after Wednesday's sharp reversal from a 14-month low near $3,425, while Ray Dalio's recommendation of a 10% to 15% gold allocation drew renewed attention. Silver rose about 1.2%. Brent crude traded around $91 a barrel after a tanker reported a nearby explosion from an unknown projectile 50 nautical miles west of Dubai late on Wednesday, the latest in a string of attacks on Gulf shipping. Bitcoin rose about 3% to around $61,000.

Ahead

US stock and bond markets are closed for Thanksgiving, and Friday is a shortened session. Thin liquidity may keep moves exaggerated into the weekend.

item.title: Heads up: Thanksgiving holiday leaves dip buyers in limbo
item.description:
The turkey couldn't have come at a more awkward time for Wall Street, could it?

Just as things were starting to get interesting again after yesterday's impressive recovery, US traders are now off to enjoy their Thanksgiving break.

As a reminder, US stock and bond markets will be closed today in observance of Thanksgiving. And even though trading resumes tomorrow, Wall Street will only be open until 1800 GMT (1pm ET) while the bond market will wrap things up at 1900 GMT (2pm ET).

But in reality, many market participants will already have one foot out the door until Monday. So, one can reasonably expect thinner liquidity conditions across broader markets over the next two days - especially during US trading hours.

That being said, let's not mistake a lack of liquidity for a lack of volatility.

With fewer buyers and sellers around, it takes considerably less money to move markets. Any relatively modest order size or unexpected headlines could make for some rather exaggerated moves in currencies, gold and stock futures.

And given how fragile the market sentiment is looking this week, I'd be particularly wary of reading too much into any technical breakouts or breakdowns during the coming two days.

As much as the turnaround yesterday was quite encouraging, the real test for dip buyers will be whether they can continue to build on that momentum once the usual crowd returns next week. All eyes will be on tech stocks to see if they can sustain a more meaningful recovery from here, or is this just another half-hearted attempt at buying the dip like we saw on Monday?

In any case, we will have to wait until the start of next week to have better clarity on all of that.

In the meantime, just remember that you are not obliged to chase every move on your screen. The next two days could offer some trading opportunities but they could just as easily serve up a few nasty traps. So, be careful out there.

At times, following the market in enjoying a little time off isn't such a bad idea. As mentioned earlier this week, there will always be another opportunity to make money in markets. And you don't have to rush in to try and pick the bottom to do that.

item.title: My Nvidia stock analysis shows bulls are better than what most seem to think
item.description:
Nvidia stock is rebuilding its bullish case. Can buyers get back above $155?

Nvidia has broken out of its recent descending channel, reclaimed two important trading areas and outperformed Nasdaq futures during its latest recovery. The next test is whether buyers can make those gains stick.

Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) is giving bulls a few more reasons to stay constructive heading into the Thanksgiving holiday.

After falling to $141.17 on Wednesday, Nvidia recovered to $151.22 by the end of after-hours trading, a rebound of approximately 7.1% from the day's low. The stock had closed the regular session at $149.30, down 3.91%.

The recovery is also starting to make more sense from a technical perspective.

Three things Nvidia bulls have achieved

Looking at my hourly Nvidia chart, there are three encouraging developments, numbered accordingly.

1. Back inside the earnings value area

A value area is a price range in which a substantial proportion of trading volume took place during a selected period.

When a stock falls below its earnings-related value area, it suggests that the market is exploring lower prices. Returning inside that area is an early indication that the rejection of those previously accepted prices may be losing strength.

Nvidia has now achieved that.

2. Breaking out of the descending channel

Nvidia has escaped the blue descending channel on the chart and returned to its previous value area.

The combination is more encouraging than a channel breakout alone. Buyers have managed to interrupt the recent downward price structure while reclaiming territory where substantial trading previously occurred.

3. Approaching the earnings point of control

The point of control (PoC), represented by the red horizontal line, is the price at which the greatest trading volume occurred within the period being analyzed.

Think of it as a historical center of trading activity. It can attract price and become an area of contention between buyers and sellers.

Nvidia is approaching that area, around $153. Sustaining prices above it would represent another achievement for the bulls.

Nvidia is also showing some relative strength

Between 3 p.m. and 8 p.m. ET on November 25, Nvidia gained approximately 2.29%, compared with 0.74% for Nasdaq-100 futures.

That is an outperformance of 1.55 percentage points.

Admittedly, part of that recovery occurred outside regular trading hours. Still, Nvidia's ability to outperform the broader technology market during this particular window adds some credibility to the rebound.

As investingLive's Greg Michalowski noted in his latest Nasdaq technical analysis, both the Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq-100 recovered sharply after testing support on Wednesday.

Four Nvidia stock price areas I am watching

  • $152.25 to $152.50: Immediate resistance. Sustaining prices above this area would strengthen the recovery case and bring the earnings PoC into play.

  • $155 to $155.50: The bigger test, incorporating Nvidia's November 17 closing price of $155.46, just before its earnings reaction. Reclaiming this area could change the broader technical picture.

  • $149 to $150.60: The first potential support area should Nvidia experience another pullback.

  • $147.50 to $147.75: A deeper area where buyers may attempt to regain control. Actual buying strength would need to emerge there.

A rejection near $152.50 followed by a failure to defend the first support area would weaken my bullish assessment.

Conversely, a break above resistance followed by a successful retest would be a healthy development.

Could bearish market positioning work in Nvidia's favor?

There are some interesting developments beyond the Nvidia chart.

Goldman Sachs reports that hedge funds have aggressively increased their short exposure, with a rise of approximately 19 percentage points in ETF shorts in a single week.

If equity prices stabilize, some of those traders may need to buy back their short positions, potentially accelerating a recovery.

Meanwhile, Citi points to extreme investor fear, noting that the S&P 500 was higher six months later in 13 of the previous 14 instances when the VIX reached 40.

Neither observation guarantees a market bottom, nor does the broader positioning data establish that Nvidia itself is heavily shorted. But both offer some perspective on the potential for a recovery.

AI investment continues, despite legitimate concerns about Nvidia

Australia's latest economic figures offer another interesting piece of the puzzle. Business investment surged 12.2% in the third quarter, with data centers and technology investment playing a prominent role.

And for a perspective on what this computing infrastructure could eventually enable, read Adam Button's thought-provoking piece on AI and recent developments in mathematics.

The technological opportunity remains considerable. Whether that opportunity translates into sufficient financial returns to justify current AI investments and stock valuations is a different question.

Nvidia also faces company-specific risks. S&P has placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade, while Moody's has maintained its rating. Governance, management oversight and dependence on Jensen Huang remain legitimate investor concerns.

What Nvidia shareholders might consider

Investors uncomfortable with their exposure do not necessarily need to make an all-or-nothing decision.

Reducing part of an oversized position near resistance is one possibility. Another is maintaining exposure while monitoring whether Nvidia can establish support at higher prices.

Active traders considering selling some shares with the intention of buying them back at lower prices should also be prepared for the possibility that their desired pullback never arrives.

My Nvidia stock outlook

investingLive Tactical Recovery Score: +5/10 (moderately bullish)

This is my subjective directional assessment for the next one to three trading sessions, not a statistical probability of further gains.

For now, the bulls are doing fine. They have reclaimed two areas of value, escaped a descending channel and are approaching the earnings point of control.

They haven't repaired the entire post-earnings decline, but they are making progress.

item.title: Ray Dalio's 10-15% gold call resurfaces as bullion tries to find its feet
item.description:
High-profile endorsements like Dalio's rarely move gold on their own, but they can support retail and wealth-management demand at a time when prices have fallen sharply and some investors are reassessing their allocations. The renewed coverage also coincides with Wednesday's reversal off a 14-month low, which may encourage dip-buyers already watching the $3,500 area. The bigger near-term drivers remain real yields, the dollar and Fed rate expectations, so the long-term case Dalio describes is unlikely to stop short-term swings. For crypto, his skepticism about bitcoin as a reserve asset adds to a debate that matters for long-term institutional demand.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold claws back $160 from a 14-month low, but one candle doesn't necessarily make a bottom
  • Gold bulls may have been waiting months for a chart like this

---

Ray Dalio isn't telling anyone when to buy gold, only how much to hold, and after this year's slide that distinction is getting a fresh hearing.

Summary:

  • Ray Dalio's comments on Nicole Lapin's Money Rehab podcast, aired around November 9, have been widely picked up over the past day or so
  • He recommends a 10% to 15% gold allocation as a permanent diversifier, regardless of market expectations
  • Dalio links the case to rising US debt, now above $40 trillion, which he likens to plaque building up in arteries
  • He prefers gold to crypto because central banks can hold gold, while crypto can be monitored and seized, though he holds some bitcoin
  • The coverage comes as gold rebounds from a 14-month low near $3,425, still about a third below its January record
  • Forecasts remain split, with Natixis warning of $3,340 and UBS targeting $5,000 by end-2027

Ray Dalio's case for keeping 10% to 15% of a portfolio in gold is getting a second wind. Comments the Bridgewater Associates founder made on Nicole Lapin's Money Rehab podcast earlier this month have been picked up widely across financial and crypto media over the past day or so, just as bullion tries to recover from its lowest level in more than a year.

The interview aired around November 9, and the view itself isn't new. Dalio has recommended the same range before, including in August. What has changed is the backdrop. Gold fell to around $3,425 an ounce on Wednesday, its weakest since September 2025, before rebounding to close near $3,590, and it remains roughly a third below its January record.

A permanent holding, not a trade

Dalio's argument is about portfolio construction rather than timing. He recommends that investors hold gold in a 10% to 15% range whether they expect good or bad times for markets, treating it as a permanent diversifier rather than a bet on direction.

His reasoning rests on debt. Dalio has compared rising US government debt, now more than $40 trillion, to plaque building up in arteries, warning that the country is very exposed to a financial "heart attack" as interest costs crowd out other spending. In that kind of environment, he argues, printing money doesn't create wealth but erodes the value of money, and that is where gold earns its place.

Gold over crypto

Asked about crypto, Dalio said he finds gold the more appealing diversifier. He does hold some bitcoin, less than his gold, and declined to say how much. His main objection is about who can own each asset. Central banks can hold gold themselves, while crypto holdings can be monitored and legally seized, which he sees as a barrier to bitcoin becoming a reserve asset. He also leaned on the old observation that gold is the one asset that doesn't depend on anyone else's promise.

Why it lands now

The renewed attention reflects a split in the gold debate. In the short term, the outlook is clouded by a Federal Reserve that is still raising rates, a strong dollar and signs that central bank buying is slowing, and Natixis has warned gold could fall to $3,340 by January. Over the longer term, banks such as UBS still see $5,000 by the end of 2027, citing the same themes Dalio highlights, including sovereign debt and reserve diversification.

Dalio's framework sits firmly on the long-term side. It offers no view on where gold goes next week, and it would have recommended the same allocation at January's record high as at Wednesday's low. For investors, that is the practical point. His case is about how much gold to own, not when to buy it, which makes it a useful anchor after a fall of this size but not a signal that the bottom is in. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Franklin Templeton adds Hyperliquid's HYPE to its EZPZ crypto index ETF from December 1
item.description:
The actual buying will be very small. At index weight, EZPZ's HYPE position should be worth well under $1 million, so there's no direct effect on the token, on bitcoin or ether, or on crypto equities such as COIN and MSTR. The real effect is on credibility. HYPE now has a place in a third diversified index product, which strengthens its claim to be a large-cap asset alongside XRP and Solana. That matters for future index rebalances and for advisers who only buy through ETFs. Sentiment is the counterweight: the dedicated HYPE ETFs have had recent outflows, and the token is about 28% below its late-August level. Investors are watching more than they are buying.

-

Another big fund manager is making room for Hyperliquid, but the amount involved is tiny and the token's price is going the other way.

Summary:

  • Franklin Crypto Index ETF (EZPZ) will begin holding HYPE on or around December 1, per a November 25 SEC prospectus supplement
  • HYPE is the only new constituent of CF Benchmarks' Institutional Digital Asset Index, announced November 16; the fund will hold eight assets
  • HYPE's starting weight was not disclosed; EZPZ had about $17.02 million in net assets at end-September, around 76% in bitcoin
  • Hashdex's NCIQ added HYPE at a 3.36% weight from September 1, and the Bitwise 10 Crypto Index ETF added it in July
  • Three US spot HYPE ETFs hold under $250 million combined; cumulative inflows top $259 million despite recent outflows
  • HYPE traded around $60 on November 25, down from about $83 in late August, though still up more than 120% this year

Franklin Templeton's Franklin Crypto Index ETF (EZPZ) will start holding Hyperliquid's HYPE token on or around December 1, according to a prospectus supplement filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on November 25. HYPE will be the only new name in the fund's lineup, taking it to eight assets alongside bitcoin, ether, XRP, Solana, Dogecoin, Cardano and Stellar.

The change follows a November 16 notice from CF Benchmarks naming HYPE as the sole new constituent of its Institutional Digital Asset Index, which EZPZ tracks. The fund holds each asset at roughly its index weight and rebalances quarterly, so buying HYPE is an automatic index step, not a decision by Franklin. The filing does not disclose HYPE's starting weight.

Scale matters here. EZPZ had about $17.02 million in net assets at the end of September, with bitcoin making up around 76% of the portfolio and ether close to 13%, according to fund data cited by crypto.news. As a rough illustration, a weight similar to the 3.36% HYPE received in Hashdex's Nasdaq CME Crypto Index ETF (NCIQ) in September would amount to only around $600,000 of the token. The addition shows where index products are heading. It won't add meaningful demand.

Index adoption is spreading. Hashdex added HYPE to NCIQ from September 1, and the Bitwise 10 Crypto Index ETF added it in July. Three US spot HYPE ETFs launched this year now hold under $250 million in assets between them, The Block reported. Cumulative inflows into HYPE ETFs have topped $259 million despite a recent stretch of outflows.

The price has not kept pace with the institutional interest. HYPE traded around $60 on November 25, well below the roughly $83 it fetched when Hashdex's inclusion was announced in late August. Even so, The Block reports the token is still up more than 120% on the year and ranks among the 10 largest cryptocurrencies, with a market value of about $13.6 billion.

Regulation is the bigger thread. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said on November 19 that onchain platforms like Hyperliquid can reach US retail users either by partnering with an existing exchange or by obtaining their own. Payward, Kraken's parent company, is already pursuing a partnership route for decentralized derivatives venues. The next things to watch are HYPE's disclosed weight once EZPZ rebalances, whether flows into the dedicated HYPE ETFs turn positive again, and any concrete step by Hyperliquid toward a licensed US channel. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: S&P puts Nvidia's AA rating on watch for a possible cut, as Moody's holds steady
item.description:
A one-notch downgrade from AA would barely change Nvidia's borrowing costs, so the bond market impact is likely to be small. For equities, the risk is reputational: S&P's focus on whether export rules were broken or China exposure was understated puts a new question mark over a stock already swinging on governance headlines. The split between S&P and Moody's could keep Nvidia's credit default swaps volatile after this week's record highs. Investors will now watch for any board changes, such as new independent directors or a formal succession plan, that could head off a downgrade.

---

Moody's looked at Nvidia's balance sheet and stood pat, while S&P looked at the boardroom and reached for the watch list.

Summary:

  • S&P placed Nvidia's AA issuer and senior unsecured debt ratings on CreditWatch negative, with a possible downgrade within 90 days
  • It expects any cut to be limited to one notch unless investigations or disclosures show damage to Nvidia's reputation or business
  • S&P cited concerns about board independence, oversight of the chief executive, succession planning and key-man risk
  • It lowered its management and governance assessment to neutral from positive
  • S&P said it would view any export-control violations or understated China disclosures as negative for credit quality
  • Moody's kept its Aa1 rating and stable outlook on the same day

S&P Global Ratings has placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on CreditWatch with negative implications, warning that it could cut the rating within 90 days over concerns about the chipmaker's management and governance. The move contrasts with Moody's, which kept its rating and stable outlook unchanged on the same day.

The decision, announced on Wednesday, covers both Nvidia's issuer rating and the rating on its senior unsecured debt. S&P said it expects any downgrade to be limited to one notch, which would still leave Nvidia with a very strong investment-grade rating. A deeper cut is possible, however, if investigations or disclosures lead the agency to conclude that Nvidia's reputation or future business has been damaged.

Why S&P is worried

S&P said recent events, including news about the chief executive and questions about potential export-control violations, have exposed weaknesses in how Nvidia is overseen. Its concerns focus on the board. The agency said the long tenure of some directors may have compromised their independence, and that governance practices may not have kept pace with Nvidia's rapid growth and its role as a critical global technology supplier.

It also pointed to a lack of succession planning and weak oversight of the chief executive, which have pushed "key man" risk to the forefront. Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 and was reinstated by the board on November 23. S&P said that sequence doesn't fully answer its questions about how the board oversees executive conduct, and that it isn't aware of any steps the board has taken to fix what could be meaningful shortcomings. As a result, S&P cut its assessment of Nvidia's management and governance to neutral from positive.

China is the bigger risk

The business itself hasn't changed in S&P's view. It said Nvidia's competitive position, technology leadership and finances are unchanged, though stricter export controls could reduce future growth. The sharper warning concerns China. If S&P comes to believe that export rules were circumvented or broken, or that Nvidia's past disclosures about its exposure to China and nearby regions were misleading or understated, that would weigh on its view of the company's overall credit quality.

S&P plans to meet Nvidia's board and management to discuss how they intend to address board independence, oversight and leadership succession.

Two agencies, two readings

The split between the agencies is notable. Moody's, which already rates Nvidia a notch higher at Aa1, said Huang's return restores strategic continuity and kept a stable outlook, while flagging key-person risk and unresolved governance questions. S&P has gone a step further by putting its rating on formal watch, which signals a real chance of action.

For investors, Nvidia's ability to repay its debt isn't in question, and S&P itself says the company's finances are unchanged. A one-notch cut would likely have limited direct impact on its borrowing costs. The bigger issue for shareholders is what a downgrade would signal. It would put governance and China compliance at the centre of the Nvidia story, at a time when gauges of the company's credit risk are already at record highs and the AI trade is under pressure.

The next 90 days will be shaped by S&P's talks with the board, any changes Nvidia makes to its governance, and the outcome of investigations into the company's conduct.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bank of Korea signals more hikes as 15 of 21 rate projections sit above 3.25%
item.description:
The projections lift the risk that Korean rates peak above the 3.50% most economists expected, which should support the won and keep short-dated Korean government bond yields firm. Two dissents limit the hawkish reading and leave room for the governor's tone to swing sentiment either way. For equities, the higher-for-longer message weighs on rate-sensitive sectors such as property and consumer stocks, while chipmakers remain driven by global AI demand. The bank's focus on household lending also raises the chance of tighter lending rules alongside rate hikes.

---

  • Bank of Korea hikes to 3.25%, sees 4.1% growth in 2027 as chip boom drives economy

- The Bank of Korea's vote was split, but its projections weren't: most of the board expects rates to keep rising.

Summary:

  • Board members Lee Soo-hyung and Hwang Kun-il dissented from the hike to 3.25%
  • Of 21 rate projections for the next six months, 6 are at 3.25%, 8 at 3.50% and 7 at 3.75%
  • The bank said the timing of further hikes will depend on inflation, the economy and financial stability
  • Inflation is expected to stay above target for a prolonged period, depending on oil prices and the exchange rate
  • Household lending growth has picked up and house price expectations remain elevated
  • Strong semiconductor-led exports and investment support growth, though the extent of the chip expansion is the key uncertainty

The Bank of Korea's decision to raise interest rates on Thursday wasn't unanimous, but the board's own projections point to more tightening ahead, with most members expecting rates to be higher in six months' time.

The central bank lifted its base rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.25%, its third increase since July. Board members Lee Soo-hyung and Hwang Kun-il dissented. The bank didn't say in its initial statement which way they would have voted, so it isn't yet clear whether they favored holding rates or a different move.

A hawkish set of projections

The bigger signal for markets came from the board's rate projections for the next six months. Of 21 projections, only 6 put the base rate at today's 3.25%. Eight placed it at 3.50%, implying one more hike, and seven at 3.75%, implying two. That means 15 of the 21 projections sit above the current rate.

That leans more hawkish than expectations going into the meeting. A Reuters poll before the decision showed economists expecting one final hike to 3.50% in early 2027. The projections suggest a meaningful share of the board sees a higher peak than that.

The policy statement backs up that message. The bank said the timing of further base rate hikes will depend on inflation trends, domestic economic conditions and financial stability. That language assumes more increases are coming rather than asking whether they're needed.

Inflation and housing keep pressure on

The central bank expects inflation to stay above its 2% target for a prolonged period, as elevated cost pressures continue to feed through to prices. It said the outlook will depend on global oil prices and the exchange rate, both of which have been pushing prices higher this year.

Financial stability is the other concern. The bank said growth in household lending has picked up, expectations of further house price gains remain elevated, and risks of financial imbalances linked to housing and household debt need continued monitoring.

On growth, the bank was confident. It expects the economy to sustain robust growth, with exports and investment supported by the semiconductor sector. It did flag one clear uncertainty: how far the expansion in semiconductors will go.

What it means for markets

For the Korean won and short-term bond yields, the projections matter more than the dissents. A board that sees rates at 3.50% or 3.75% within six months gives the won some support and argues against any early easing, although the two dissents show the board isn't of one mind.

The link to chips cuts both ways. Strong semiconductor demand is driving the growth that allows the bank to keep tightening. If the global AI spending cycle slows, the same sector would weaken the economy and the case for further hikes, which is why the bank singled it out as the main uncertainty. Governor Rhee Chang-yong's comments at his news conference should help clarify which way the dissenters leaned and how firmly the board is committed to the next move.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman says hedge funds pile into shorts, with ETF shorts posting a 19-point weekly jump

Low hedge fund positioning cuts both ways. It limits the pool of forced sellers if the selloff resumes, but it also means a stabilization in prices could trigger short covering and re-risking that lifts stocks faster than fundamentals alone would suggest. The steady $150 billion of retail and retirement inflows provides a floor under large-cap indices, especially the mega-cap names those funds hold most. Homebuilders and other consumer-cyclical stocks with crowded shorts could be the most volatile if sentiment turns. With US markets closed for Thanksgiving, any re-risking is unlikely to show up until next week.

----

Wednesday:

  • investingLive Americas FX news wrap 25 Nov: It’s a Wrap. S&P 500 and Nasdaq pare steep losses

---

Professional investors are hedged and waiting for prices to stabilize, while retirement savers keep buying, and that split could shape how the next rally unfolds.

Summary:

  • Goldman's Vincent Lin says hedge funds cut exposure for five straight weeks, then added short positions in stocks, index futures and ETFs
  • ETF shorts rose about 19 percentage points in a week, the third-largest weekly increase in a decade
  • Clients rotated toward staples, utilities and REITs, favored hyperscalers within tech and shorted homebuilders
  • Hedge fund and trend-following positioning is near multi-year lows, while ETF and mutual funds took in about $150 billion in a month
  • Fundamental long-short funds were up about 7% this year, down from about 17% at midyear
  • Lin still favors hyperscalers and healthcare over consumer staples, and is watching tech earnings, payrolls, CPI and the Fed

Hedge funds have moved from cutting risk to actively betting against the market, according to Goldman Sachs, a sign of how fragile sentiment has become during this month's selloff in technology stocks.

Vincent Lin, co-head of Prime Insights and Analytics in Goldman's FICC and Equities business, said on the bank's The Markets podcast that hedge fund clients reduced their exposure for five straight weeks. Last week the selling stopped, but clients turned more defensive by adding short positions in individual stocks and in index futures and ETFs. ETF short positions rose by about 19 percentage points in a single week, the third-largest weekly increase in the past decade. The episode was recorded on November 23, before Wednesday's US inflation data.

Where the money is moving

The rotation has favored defensive sectors. Consumer staples, utilities and real estate investment trusts have clearly outperformed over the past month, helped by lower volatility, less reliance on consumer spending and little connection to the AI trade. Within technology, clients have preferred the biggest cloud and AI platform companies, known as hyperscalers, for their stronger balance sheets and steadier earnings. On the short side, they have targeted economically sensitive consumer areas, especially housing and homebuilders, where positioning has fallen to multi-year lows.

Fast money retreats, slow money keeps buying

Lin drew a sharp contrast between types of investors. Hedge funds and trend-following funds are near the bottom of their historical positioning ranges, and retail day traders have pulled back. But slower-moving retirement and mutual fund investors remain heavily invested, with ETF and mutual fund products taking in about $150 billion over the past month even as markets fell.

That gap matters for the near-term outlook. Lin said that when uncertainty is high, buyers tend to wait for higher prices before stepping back in. Hedge fund managers want to see prices stabilize before adding risk, and with the year nearly over, many are focused on protecting gains rather than chasing a rally. His models point to more supportive flows if prices steady or start trending higher.

Why hedge funds are cautious

Lin pointed to two drivers. The first is performance. Fundamental long-short equity funds were up about 17% at midyear but only about 7% at the time of recording, which he characterized as a setback rather than a collapse. The second is the AI story itself. Lin said "the best of the AI infrastructure returns is probably behind us," and that the trade is shifting toward how companies make money from AI, a transition he noted has historically been the hardest phase of major technology cycles.

He remains constructive on parts of the market. Lin still favors the hyperscalers and argues they should be relative winners if computing capacity stays tight, adding that any slowdown in AI spending could free up cash for buybacks. He also prefers healthcare over consumer staples, citing more attractive valuations and earnings drivers less tied to AI.

What to watch

Lin flagged late-season tech earnings, US payrolls next week and November inflation data in about three weeks as the key tests, along with whether the Federal Reserve's hawkish stance holds. Since the recording, hotter-than-expected core PCE inflation has kept a December hike firmly priced. That leaves the near-term backdrop little changed for cautious hedge funds.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The RBA's three 'stars' are fuzzier than they look: what it means for AUD and stocks
item.description:
The article doesn't signal any change in policy, but it supports the RBA's data-dependent approach, and that has practical consequences for traders. When the central bank can't be confident where neutral sits, the market's estimate of the peak cash rate is likely to stay unsettled, which tends to mean larger swings in short-term Australian bond yields and the Australian dollar around major data. The same debate is playing out at the Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan, so uncertainty over neutral rates is a global source of volatility in rate expectations, not just a local one.

---

Earlier:

  • Australia's data centre boom drives the biggest capex jump in years, near mining-boom highs

---

The RBA has admitted, in some detail, that it can't see its guiding stars clearly, which is exactly why traders should watch the data the central bank is watching.

Summary:

  • An article in the RBA's November Bulletin examines the uncertainty around three "star" variables: the NAIRU, potential output and the neutral interest rate
  • It finds that the usual measure of uncertainty, the range of estimates across models, captures only part of the true uncertainty
  • The neutral rate is the most uncertain, with model estimates often spanning 2 to 3 percentage points
  • Estimates can be revised substantially, by as much as half a percentage point for the NAIRU, including for past periods
  • The broad direction can still be clear: the RBA's models gave only a very small chance that unemployment was above the NAIRU between 2023 and 2025
  • Research cited in the article suggests relying more on observed data when star variables are uncertain, which raises the market importance of each data release

Central banks steer interest rates partly by reference to benchmarks no one can see. A new article from the Reserve Bank of Australia explains just how uncertain those benchmarks are, and the answer matters for anyone trading the Australian dollar, bonds or local stocks.

The article, "Uncertainty About the Stars" by RBA economists Leon Berkelmans and Matthew Read, appears in the November edition of the RBA Bulletin, published on Thursday. Its central message is that the "star" variables policymakers use to judge how hot the economy is running are much harder to pin down than commonly used measures suggest, and that the neutral interest rate is the hardest of all.

What is the RBA Bulletin?

The Bulletin is one of the RBA's regular publications. It is released quarterly at 11:30am Sydney time (0030 GMT), with articles also published on an ad hoc basis, and it carries analysis of economic and financial developments as well as articles on the RBA's history and operations. This edition contains two articles, one on small business conditions and this one on star variables.

The Bulletin isn't a policy statement. The articles are written by RBA staff and reflect their research rather than a decision of the Monetary Policy Board. They are still worth reading, because they show how the bank thinks about the economy and which tools sit behind its decisions.

What are the "stars"?

The article covers three benchmarks, often written with a star symbol:

  • The NAIRU: the unemployment rate consistent with low and stable inflation. If unemployment falls below it, wage and price pressure tends to build.
  • Potential output: the level of GDP the economy can sustain without generating inflation. The gap between actual output and this level is the output gap.
  • The neutral interest rate: the inflation-adjusted cash rate that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. A policy rate above neutral is restrictive, and one below it is stimulatory.

None can be observed directly. They must be estimated with economic models, so they come with error bands.

What the RBA found

The authors show that the usual shortcut for measuring uncertainty, the range of estimates across the RBA's suite of models, gives a misleading sense of precision. The RBA's six NAIRU models currently differ by only about 0.15 percentage points, yet the uncertainty band within the models spans about a full percentage point. Estimates also get revised as new data arrive, by as much as half a percentage point for the NAIRU, and those revisions often change the past as well as the present. The latest update raised the NAIRU estimate, but the authors stress that this was a reassessment of its level rather than a sign it had risen during the quarter.

The neutral rate is the most uncertain of the three. Estimates from different models have often spanned 2 to 3 percentage points, a range the authors describe as large compared with normal movements in the real cash rate.

There is an important reassurance. Uncertainty about the exact level of a benchmark doesn't always mean uncertainty about the direction of the economy. The RBA's models gave only a very small chance that unemployment was above the NAIRU between 2023 and 2025, meaning the labour market was clearly tight even if no one knew exactly how tight.

What it means for traders

The most important point for markets comes in the article's discussion of policy. It cites research suggesting that when star variables are highly uncertain, policymakers should put more weight on observed data such as inflation and changes in unemployment. Treating uncertain estimates as precise risks large policy mistakes.

For traders, that translates into three practical points:

  • Data releases carry more weight. With the cash rate at 4.85% after five hikes this year, the RBA can't say with confidence how far above neutral it is. That makes inflation, jobs and activity data the main guide to its next move, which tends to mean sharper moves in short-term yields and the Australian dollar on surprises.
  • The peak rate is a wide range. If the neutral rate could sit anywhere in a band several percentage points wide, so could the eventual peak in rates. Market pricing for the RBA's path can shift quickly, and the Australian dollar often moves with it, especially relative to the US dollar while the Federal Reserve is also raising rates.
  • Rate-sensitive stocks feel it first. Banks, property trusts and consumer stocks on the ASX tend to react most to changes in the expected path of rates, so data-driven repricing usually shows up there before it reaches the broader index.

Australia isn't alone. Bank of Japan staff put Japan's neutral rate somewhere between 1.1% and 2.5%, and that ambiguity has fed directly into yen volatility. The lesson travels well: when a central bank can't locate neutral, the market's best guide is the same data the central bank is watching.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BoJ's Tamura says rates must reach neutral 'soon', still sees neutral near 2%
item.description:
With a December hike already largely priced, the speech matters mainly for expectations of where the cycle ends. Tamura's 2% neutral estimate sits at the top of the market's assumed endpoint of 1.75% to 2%, so any sign that his view is spreading on the board would lift Japanese government bond yields at the short end and support the yen. Yen bears may test how much the BoJ is willing to do, with USD/JPY near 159 and intervention risk in the background. His explicit openness to accelerating hikes makes upcoming Tokyo CPI and wage data more sensitive for the yen.

Newswire cut: BoJ hawk Tamura says rates must reach neutral soon and still puts neutral near 2%, well above the 1.25% policy rate. He warns Japan's less firmly anchored inflation could require a faster pace of rate hikes if upside price pressures keep building.

One-line wrap: Tamura wants the BoJ to get to neutral soon and believes neutral is a long way above today's rate, which makes him the clearest voice on the board for a longer hiking cycle.

Summary:

  • BoJ board member Naoki Tamura said the policy rate should be brought to neutral "soon", and he still puts neutral at around 2%
  • He said financial conditions remain accommodative, with the 1.25% policy rate "still some way" from neutral
  • He described the approach as "make haste slowly" and said the BoJ could assess each hike's effects within a few months
  • Tamura said weaker anchoring of inflation expectations means the BoJ should respond faster to overshoots, including by speeding up hikes
  • He cited producer prices up 7.1% from a year earlier and CPI excluding temporary measures at around 3.5% as signs of upside risk
  • He said AI-related demand is boosting a much wider range of Japanese industries than he expected

Bank of Japan board member Naoki Tamura called on Thursday for interest rates to rise to a neutral level "soon". He repeated his view that neutral sits around 2% and warned that the central bank may need to speed up its hikes if inflation pressures build.

Tamura, one of the board's most hawkish members, was speaking to local leaders in Yamanashi at 0100 GMT (2000 US Eastern on Wednesday). His remarks reinforce expectations of a rate rise at the BoJ's December 17-18 meeting and suggest he wants further increases well into 2027.

Policy is still loose, and neutral is a long way off

The BoJ raised its short-term policy rate to around 1.25% in September. Tamura said financial conditions remain accommodative and the policy rate is "still some way" from neutral, the level that neither heats nor cools the economy. He said he first put neutral at around 2% in June and that his view hasn't changed.

That gap matters for markets. If Tamura is right, the BoJ would need roughly three more quarter-point hikes to reach neutral, more than many investors expect. He was candid that neutral can't be known in advance and can only be found by raising rates and watching how the economy responds. The point echoes the RBA's discussion of uncertainty around the neutral rate in its latest Bulletin.

Make haste slowly

Tamura described the right approach as "make haste slowly". He argued that the BoJ can judge the impact of each hike within a few months by talking to firms and reading surveys, and that a thorough assessment doesn't have to be a slow one. Most firms, he said, see the effect of past and near-term hikes on their business as limited, although some have started to warn that higher borrowing costs will restrain investment.

He also flagged the option of moving faster. Inflation expectations in Japan have only recently risen from very low levels, so Tamura said they are less firmly anchored than in the United States or Europe. In his view, that means the BoJ should respond more quickly and strongly to signs that inflation is overshooting, including by speeding up the pace of hikes.

Upside risks are building

Tamura laid out why he is worried about inflation running above the 2% target. Producer prices rose 7.1% from a year earlier in October, driven by high oil prices linked to the Middle East conflict, the weak yen and AI-related demand. Those costs are now reaching consumers. He said CPI inflation excluding temporary government measures has risen to around 3.5%, and pointed to sharp price increases in items such as plastic goods and laptops.

He was also struck by how far the AI boom reaches. He said it is helping a much wider range of Japanese industries than he expected, from data centres to power equipment, air conditioning and construction. He described Japan as rich in "pick-and-shovel" firms, the businesses that supply the tools for a boom rather than taking part in it directly, a reference to the suppliers who profited most from the California Gold Rush. He added that AI is likely to push prices up in the short term, even if it lowers them later through higher productivity.

What it means for the yen

Tamura's views are well known, so the speech is unlikely to shift December pricing much on its own. The more important signal is his push for a faster path toward 2%, which is at the top end of market pricing for an endpoint of around 1.75% to 2%. A more hawkish path would generally support the yen, which is trading near 159 per dollar, close to levels that have previously raised the risk of intervention by Japanese authorities. The weak yen is itself one of the inflation pressures Tamura cites, which makes his case for steady hikes harder to dismiss.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bank of Korea hikes to 3.25%, sees 4.1% growth in 2027 as chip boom drives economy
item.description:
With the hike fully priced, the won and Korean bonds are likely to react more to Governor Rhee's guidance than to the decision itself. A signal that one more hike is coming would support the won and push up short-term yields, while hints that the cycle is ending could ease pressure on rate-sensitive stocks. The 4.1% growth forecast for 2027 is a strong vote of confidence in chip demand, which may help steady Samsung and SK Hynix after this week's selloff, but it also ties Korea's rate path closely to the global AI spending cycle.

---

Earlier:

  • Nikkei and Kospi rebound over 1% as Asia follows Wall Street's comeback, BoK decision next

---

South Korea's central bank is raising rates into a chip boom, betting that growth above 4% can absorb tighter policy while inflation slowly returns to target.

Summary:

  • The Bank of Korea raised its base rate by 25 basis points to 3.25%, in line with a Reuters poll
  • It's the third hike since July, after a pause at 3% in October
  • The bank forecasts growth of 3.9% in 2026, 4.1% in 2027 and 3.0% in 2028
  • Inflation is projected at 2.7% in 2026, 2.4% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028
  • A semiconductor export boom and rising Seoul home prices underpin the tightening
  • Markets now await Governor Rhee's guidance, with economists expecting one more hike to 3.50% in early 2027

The Bank of Korea raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.25% on Thursday, its third increase since July. A semiconductor-led export boom is keeping the economy growing strongly and inflation above target.

The decision, announced at around 0100 GMT (2000 US Eastern on Wednesday), matched expectations, with 32 of 34 economists in a Reuters poll forecasting the move. It follows back-to-back hikes in July and August and a pause at 3% in October, when the board kept its tightening bias.

New forecasts underline the strength

Alongside the decision, the central bank released updated projections that show an economy running well above its usual pace. It now expects growth of 3.9% this year and 4.1% in 2027, before easing to 3.0% in 2028. Inflation is forecast at 2.7% this year, slowing to 2.4% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028, so it only gets close to the bank's 2% target by the end of the forecast period.

The inflation projections for this year and next are unchanged from the bank's August outlook, which suggests the board sees price pressures as sticky rather than worsening. Growth of more than 4% would be exceptional for South Korea, and it explains why the bank has room to keep tightening.

Chips drive the economy, and the hikes

Semiconductors sit at the centre of the story. South Korea's chip exports nearly quadrupled from a year earlier to a record in the first 20 days of November, and made up almost half of total exports. That boom has lifted incomes and investment, while home prices in Seoul have climbed sharply, adding to the central bank's concerns about financial stability.

What comes next

The focus now turns to Governor Rhee Chang-yong's guidance on whether this is the last move. Economists in the Reuters poll expected one final hike to 3.50% in early 2027, while some local surveys see the peak as high as 3.75%. Whether the board was unanimous, and whether its statement keeps language about further tightening, will shape that debate.

Market reaction has been limited so far. The Kospi was up about 1% in morning trade, recovering part of Wednesday's slide of more than 6%, as investors weighed the steady policy outlook against volatility in global chip stocks.

For markets, the risk lies in the gap between strong local fundamentals and fragile global sentiment. A chip-driven economy gives the Bank of Korea reason to keep rates higher for longer. But any reversal in global AI spending would hit the same exports that are powering growth, and could quickly change the outlook for rates. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia's data centre boom drives the biggest capex jump in years, near mining-boom highs
item.description:
The surprise is large, but the market reaction is likely to stay muted because so much of the spending is imported equipment that does little for local output or wages. Investors are more likely to focus on what it says about capacity pressure and the RBA's December decision, where any lift in hike odds would support the Australian dollar and push up short-term yields. The industry mix matters for equities: the boom is concentrated in data centres and technology rather than mining, which favours data centre operators, construction and electrical contractors, and power suppliers over the resources sector that dominated past investment cycles.

---

Australia's investment boom is back near mining-boom highs, but this time it's being built from server racks rather than iron ore mines.

Summary:

  • Private capex rose 12.2% in the September quarter, against a 4.4% forecast and a 3.6% fall in Q2, and was up 18.6% from a year earlier
  • Equipment, plant and machinery spending rose 23.1% to a record, while buildings and structures rose 1.7%
  • Investment in information media and telecommunications, which includes data centres, rose 86.7%, with equipment spending up 183.5%
  • Non-mining capex rose 16.0% against 1.4% for mining, and Victoria led the states with a 31.0% rise
  • Firms' fourth estimate of 2026-27 spending rose 11.8% to about A$224 billion, with equipment plans up 20.4%
  • Heavy reliance on imports will limit the GDP boost, and the RBA meets again on December 7-8

Australian business investment surged far beyond expectations in the third quarter. Private capital spending jumped 12.2% from the previous quarter, almost three times the 4.4% rise economists had forecast, Australian Bureau of Statistics data showed on Thursday.

The figures, released at 0030 GMT (1930 US Eastern on Wednesday), put total capex at about A$59.5 billion for the quarter in inflation-adjusted terms, 18.6% higher than a year earlier. That takes it close to the peak reached during the mining investment boom more than a decade ago.

The jump came almost entirely from equipment. Spending on plant and machinery soared 23.1% in the quarter and 34.3% from a year earlier, reversing an 8.9% fall in the June quarter and lifting it to a record. Investment in buildings and structures rose a more modest 1.7%.

The industry detail points clearly to data centres. Total investment in information media and telecommunications, the industry that includes data centres, rose 86.7% in the quarter, and its equipment spending nearly tripled, up 183.5%. Earlier this year the ABS attributed a 6.5% jump in March-quarter capex to data centre equipment such as server racks and processing gear, and the June-quarter fall was widely seen as payback. Mining investment rose just 1.4%, while non-mining capex climbed 16.0%. Victoria led the states with a 31.0% rise.

Firms also plan to keep spending. Their fourth estimate of capital expenditure for the 2026-27 financial year came in at about A$224 billion, 11.8% above the previous estimate. Planned equipment spending was revised up 20.4% to about A$102 billion, far outpacing a 5.6% upgrade for buildings and structures.

There is an important caveat. Much of that equipment is imported, so a large share of the spending flows offshore rather than adding to domestic output. The boost to Australia's GDP will therefore be considerably smaller than the headline suggests. The ABS also completed its annual seasonal review with this release, which caused minor revisions to the equipment series.

For the Reserve Bank of Australia, the data still adds to the case that the economy is running hot. The RBA raised its cash rate to 4.85% on November 3, its highest since 2008 and its fifth hike of the year, in a split 6-3 vote. The board said inflation remains broad-based and likely to stay above 3% for longer than previously expected, but it dropped its explicit warning about further increases.

The RBA's final meeting of the year concludes on December 8, with the decision due at 0330 GMT (2230 US Eastern on December 7). October inflation data and third-quarter GDP figures will carry more weight before then, but strong investment intentions make it harder for the board to argue that demand is cooling.

The figures also stand out against a global backdrop of growing resistance to data centre projects, from Tokyo's suburbs to Australia's own Northern Territory. In Australia's biggest cities, at least, the money is still being spent.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6655 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nikkei and Kospi rebound over 1% as Asia follows Wall Street's comeback, BoK decision next
item.description:
The early gains look more like relief after a heavy selloff than a new rally, so the Bank of Korea's guidance could quickly decide whether Seoul holds them. A hawkish signal on further hikes could firm the won but weigh on rate-sensitive Korean stocks. In Japan, the yen near 159 per dollar keeps intervention risk in view, and any hawkish comments from Tamura could lift the yen and trim exporter gains. Treasury yields edging higher in Asian trade are a reminder that the inflation backdrop hasn't changed, which limits how far the rebound can run without fresh support.

---

  • investingLive Americas FX news wrap 25 Nov: It’s a Wrap. S&P 500 and Nasdaq pare steep losses

---

Asia is taking its cue from Wall Street's late recovery, but with New York shut for Thanksgiving and the Bank of Korea about to speak, the rebound has little to lean on.

Summary:

  • The Nikkei 225 rose about 1.3% to around 57,700 in early trade after falling almost 3% on Wednesday
  • The Kospi gained about 1.2% to around 4,750, and the Kosdaq rose more than 2%, after the Kospi's 6% slide on Wednesday
  • Wall Street recovered from steep early losses to close higher on Wednesday
  • S&P 500 futures rose about 0.3% and Nasdaq 100 futures about 0.1%
  • Mainland China and Hong Kong open later, after both fell on Wednesday
  • The Bank of Korea decision and a speech by BoJ board member Naoki Tamura are both due around 0100 GMT

Asian stocks opened higher on Thursday, recovering part of Wednesday's heavy losses after Wall Street staged a late comeback. Thin holiday trading and a Bank of Korea rate decision are likely to keep moves cautious.

Japan's Nikkei 225 rose about 1.3% in early trade to around 57,700, after falling almost 3% on Wednesday. South Korea's Kospi gained about 1.2% to around 4,750, and the tech-heavy Kosdaq climbed more than 2%. The rebound is modest next to Wednesday's slide, when the Kospi dropped more than 6% as chip stocks were hit hard.

The lead came from New York, where stocks recovered from steep early losses to close higher on Wednesday, with the Dow erasing a drop of more than 1,000 points. The early selling had followed hotter-than-expected US core PCE inflation and strong growth data, which kept a December Federal Reserve rate hike firmly priced. US stock index futures extended the gains in Asia, with S&P 500 futures up about 0.3% and Nasdaq 100 futures up about 0.1%.

Mainland China and Hong Kong markets open at 0130 GMT, after the Shanghai Composite fell about 2% and the Hang Seng about 1% on Wednesday.

The next test for Korean stocks comes at around 0100 GMT (2000 US Eastern on Wednesday), when the Bank of Korea announces its final policy decision of the year. Economists widely expect a quarter-point hike to 3.25%, so the bank's guidance on further tightening is likely to matter more than the move itself. Bank of Japan board member Naoki Tamura, one of the board's hawks, speaks at the same time, ahead of a December meeting where markets expect a hike.

Trading is likely to be lighter than usual. US stock and bond markets are closed for Thanksgiving and Friday is a shortened session, which leaves Asian investors without a fresh lead from New York for the rest of the week. Thin liquidity can exaggerate moves on any surprise headline, whether from Seoul, Tokyo or the Gulf, where this week's tanker attacks have kept Brent crude around $91 a barrel. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
